summary: A humorous April 1st memo that proposes requirements for an imaginary Omniscience Protocol, to support legislative efforts to interfere with allegedly illegal activity online. It is a satire of such proposals, not a real protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a joke document about a pretend system that would let someone know everything people do online. It is a joke poking fun at snooping ideas.

questions: what are the omniscience protocol requirements
subtitle: An April 1st satire: requirements for a protocol that would let enforcers know what a user intends.

tldr.problem: The memo imagines legislators and copyright holders wanting to interfere with allegedly illegal activity online without hitting innocent users, which would need knowing a person's intent.
tldr.mechanism: It lists operational and functional requirements for an Omniscience Protocol in which a client on every computer answers queries from enforcement servers.
tldr.outcome: The requirements are impossible by design, such as determining intent with complete reliability, and the security section ends with the words "Good luck."

today: RFC 3751 is an Informational April 1st joke document, and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is not a real protocol.

sections.title: An April 1st Joke About Enforcement
sections.content:
RFC 3751 is an April 1st joke document, dated 1 April 2004. It quotes a 2003 U.S. Senate hearing and an earlier bill about disabling peer-to-peer file-trading networks, and observes that anyone acting on such laws would need to reduce the error rate. Part of that is determining intent, so it proposes requirements for an Omniscience Protocol (OP) to determine a person's intent.

The target of the satire is the idea of such enforcement, not a real protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Some grown-ups wanted a way to know whether someone meant to do something wrong. This memo pretends to write down the rules for a magic mind-reading machine.

sections.title: The Imagined Design
sections.content: It assumes a client-server model. The OP client is installed on the user's computer and the server is run by a law or copyright enforcement organization. Clients register with all servers for their legal jurisdiction each time the computer starts, and servers send OP Queries on whatever schedule they use. The memo jokes that future versions might use a peer-to-peer model once copyright enforcers get over their disgust at the concept.
sections.plainLanguage: Every computer would have a little spy helper that answers questions from a watching office.

sections.title: Operational and Functional Requirements
sections.content:
The operational requirements OR1 to OR5 include installing on all computers over the user's objections, being unfindable by the user including by commercial virus detectors, communicating through uncooperative firewalls and NATs even when disconnected from the Internet, and being impossible to spoof.

The functional requirements FR1 to FR9 demand the impossible: determining user intent, telling illegal copies from legal ones with complete reliability even if renamed or modified, resisting hackers, rejecting server operators whose motives are not pure, extracting no unrelated information, knowing who put material on a machine, and applying only the laws of the computer's current location. The satire works by taking each demand to its logical extreme.
sections.plainLanguage: The wish list asks for a helper that is invisible, cannot be fooled, never makes mistakes and always knows the local laws. Nobody could build that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The OP requires strong authentication of clients and servers, strong integrity technology so messages cannot be modified in flight, and strong encryption so communication cannot be observed. All of this is needed where many users have full control of their computers and are actively hostile to the protocol. The section ends with "Good luck."
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says the hard part is that the people being watched own the machines, then wishes the builders luck.
